prompt: A technician is about to open a gas-furnace control panel to replace a 240 V indoor-blower relay. The thermostat is already set to Off. What is the first safe step before any metal tool enters the panel?

options.text: Lock out and tag the disconnect, then prove the circuit dead with a meter
Trust the Off thermostat and start the swap to save a trip outside
Pull the door switch only so 24 V drops while line voltage stays on
Wear cotton work gloves and keep the circuit live for a faster swap

explanation: NATE Core electrical safety is lockout/tagout plus a proved-dead check. A thermostat Off command only opens the 24 V control path; line voltage can still sit on the transformer, relay, and blower circuit. Isolate at a lockable disconnect, tag it, and verify zero voltage with a known-good meter before tools enter the panel.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a thermostat Off command with isolation; the indoor unit can still be live at the disconnect and transformer.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the blower door interlock with lockout; that switch drops only control power and leaves lethal line voltage.
distractorExplanations.d: Cotton gloves are not electrical PPE, and working a live 240 V panel is not a time-saving method.

prompt: An installer is brazing a new copper liquid line with the circuit open to air. Which purge practice keeps oxide scale out of the tubing and avoids feeding the joint with oxygen?

options.text: Flow compressed shop air through the tubing the whole time it is heated
Flow a low stream of dry nitrogen through the tubing while heating
Hold a static 150 psig nitrogen charge in the open joint while heating
Purge with nitrogen first, then shut the flow off before the torch starts

explanation: A low-flow dry-nitrogen sweep displaces oxygen while the copper is hot, so internal oxide scale does not form and the joint is not oxygen-fed. Shop air is moist oxygen. A 150 psig static charge is a pressure-test level and blows filler from an open joint. A pre-purge alone lets air return as soon as flow stops.

distractorExplanations.a: Shop air carries oxygen and moisture, so copper oxide still forms and the flame can be oxygen-fed.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a nitrogen leak-test pressure with a braze sweep; 150 psig in an open joint ejects filler metal.
distractorExplanations.d: A pre-purge only; air re-enters as the tube heats unless nitrogen keeps flowing during heating.

prompt: A new line set is ready for a leak check before any refrigerant is weighed in. How should the installer pressure-test the piping?

options.text: Pressurize from the oxygen cylinder because that gas is dry and oil-free
Pressurize with unregulated shop air so a soap-bubble test costs less
Pressurize with dry nitrogen through a regulator; never use oxygen
Pressurize from a virgin refrigerant cylinder until bubbles stop forming

explanation: Installers leak-check with dry nitrogen and a regulator so pressure is controlled and the gas is inert. Oxygen plus compressor oil or residual organics can ignite or explode in copper piping. Shop air adds moisture. Using virgin refrigerant as a test gas wastes product and is not a controlled pressure test.

distractorExplanations.a: Oxygen in an oil-wetted or dirty line is an explosion hazard; dryness does not make oxygen a test gas.
distractorExplanations.b: Unregulated shop air can overshoot the rating and loads moisture into a circuit that must stay dry.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses charging with leak testing; refrigerant is not a standing pressure-test medium for new piping.

prompt: A homeowner reports a strong rotten-egg smell around a gas furnace that has not been running. The technician has just arrived. What is the correct first action?

options.text: Start the furnace through one full cycle to see whether the odor clears
Flip the blower switch so room air dilutes the odor, then hunt the leak
Inspect the flue first, because that odor always means combustion spillage
Shut the gas, ventilate without making sparks, and treat it as a leak

explanation: Mercaptan odorant means unburned fuel gas until proved otherwise. Kill the gas supply, ventilate by opening doors and windows, and keep ignition sources off—including light switches, motors, and the furnace itself—until the area is safe and the leak is found. Combustion products such as CO are largely odorless and are not what mercaptan signals.

distractorExplanations.a: Lighting burners in a gas-odor space is an ignition source; the odor itself is a stop-and-ventilate cue.
distractorExplanations.b: Switching a blower or other load can spark; dilution is done with gas off and no electrical switching.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses mercaptan (unburned gas) with flue spillage; CO and other combustion gases are not rotten-egg scented.

prompt: A tech will service a natural-gas furnace in a tight attic with limited combustion openings. What must be in place before work starts?

options.text: Combustion-air path, CO awareness, and a planned way out of the space
A dust mask, which also filters carbon monoxide during the visit
Tape over combustion-air openings so the attic stays more comfortable
A spotter only if the appliance is a sealed hydronic boiler, not a furnace

explanation: NATE Core confined-space practice around fuel-fired equipment is combustion air, carbon monoxide awareness, and an exit plan before the tech is committed in an attic or crawl. Particulate masks do not stop CO. Blocking combustion air starves the burner and raises CO. Any fuel-fired appliance in an enclosed space can produce CO, not only boilers.

distractorExplanations.b: N95-style dust filters do not remove CO; that risk is handled with air, monitoring, and egress—not a mask.
distractorExplanations.c: Sealing combustion air starves the furnace and can drive incomplete combustion and CO into the attic.
distractorExplanations.d: CO and egress apply to a gas furnace in a tight attic the same way they apply to other fuel-fired appliances.

prompt: On a package unit, the dual run capacitor is cracked and bulged. What is the safe replacement practice?

options.text: Match microfarads but drop the voltage rating if the can is a tighter fit
Discharge it, then replace with the specified MFD and voltage rating
Install a higher MFD can so the compressor and fan get extra torque
Leave it in service if a meter still shows MFD within six percent

explanation: A bulged or cracked capacitor has a failed dielectric and can still hold a shock charge. Short the terminals with an insulated tool after power is off, then install a can that matches specified microfarads and equals or exceeds the voltage rating. Oversizing MFD overheats start windings. A passing MFD reading does not make a vented case safe.

distractorExplanations.a: A lower voltage rating than the original can fail early; voltage must meet or exceed the specified rating.
distractorExplanations.c: Extra MFD raises winding current and heat; replacements stay on the specified microfarad value.
distractorExplanations.d: A cracked or bulged case is a failed part even if capacitance still reads near the label.

prompt: An installer is setting up oxy-acetylene to braze a filter-drier in a mechanical room. Which setup is required before the torch is lit?

options.text: Crack the oxygen valve first so the flame lights with less acetylene
Oil the oxygen regulator threads so they seat without a leak
Fit flashback arrestors and keep oil and grease off oxygen fittings
Lay both cylinders on their sides so they cannot be knocked over

explanation: Oxygen under pressure plus oil or grease can ignite. Flashback arrestors and reverse-flow check valves stop a flame or oxygen from traveling back into the hoses and cylinders. Acetylene cylinders stay upright so acetone does not leave the porous mass. Lighting sequence and oily oxygen threads are common field errors that start fires.

distractorExplanations.a: Wrong lighting sequence; oxygen-first lighting and a fuel-rich start are not the safe torch procedure.
distractorExplanations.b: Oil on oxygen fittings is an ignition hazard; those threads are seated dry, never lubricated with oil.
distractorExplanations.d: Acetylene cylinders must stay upright; laying them down can release acetone into the hose and torch.

prompt: A rooftop condensing unit needs temporary 120 V for a vacuum pump after a rain. Standing water is still on the roof. How should power be supplied?

options.text: Use an indoor lamp cord; the unit ground already protects anyone on the roof
Use a heavy outdoor cord on a plain receptacle, treating GFCI as indoor-only
Cut the ground pin so a GFCI will not trip in the wet location
Avoid cords if possible; if needed, use GFCI and an outdoor-rated cord

explanation: Wet outdoor work is a ground-fault shock hazard. Prefer the unit’s own protected receptacle or postpone until the roof is dry. If temporary power is unavoidable, use a GFCI device and a cord rated for outdoor wet use. Equipment grounding of the condenser does not protect the person holding a damaged indoor cord.

distractorExplanations.a: Indoor cord jackets are not for standing water, and the unit ground does not protect the person on the cord.
distractorExplanations.b: GFCI is required in wet outdoor locations too; conductor gauge sizes ampacity, not ground-fault protection.
distractorExplanations.c: Removing the ground pin defeats the equipment-grounding path; a trip is a fault that must be found.

prompt: A belt-driven indoor blower needs a new belt. The disconnect is off. What else must be true before hands go near the pulley?

options.text: Lockout is verified and the wheel cannot free-spin into the technician
Power is restored so the tech can jog the motor and watch belt tracking
The old belt stays tightly tensioned so the new belt can be size-matched
The blower-door switch is jumped so the motor can bump for alignment

explanation: Belt and pulley work is mechanical energy control, not only electrical off. After the disconnect is locked, confirm the circuit is dead and that the blower wheel cannot store or release rotational energy into fingers. Jogging live, leaving a loaded belt, or jumping the door switch puts hands in a rotating machine.

distractorExplanations.b: Restoring power to watch tracking puts hands next to a live rotating pulley—the hazard being controlled.
distractorExplanations.c: A tensioned belt stores energy and can pinch; release tension before hands work the pulley.
distractorExplanations.d: Jumping the door interlock defeats a guard and can start the motor while hands are in the housing.

prompt: In a home garage, an open gasoline can sits next to a package unit the tech is about to power up for a charge check. What is the correct action?

options.text: Proceed; A1 refrigerants are nonflammable so a spark in the bay is fine
Remove the fuel, ventilate the bay, then do any spark-producing work
Keep a fire extinguisher at the unit and continue the electrical checks
Open the garage door and continue; vapors are assumed to leave at once

explanation: Gasoline vapor plus a contactor, meter, or motor spark is an ignition and explosion hazard, independent of the refrigerant safety class. Remove flammable liquids, ventilate until vapors are gone, then resume electrical or charging work. An extinguisher is backup, not a control. Gasoline vapor is heavier than air and can pool even with a door open.

distractorExplanations.a: Refrigerant A1 class is irrelevant here; the gasoline vapor is the fuel that a spark can ignite.
distractorExplanations.c: An extinguisher does not remove the vapor; fuels leave the space before spark-producing tasks start.
distractorExplanations.d: Heavier-than-air gasoline vapor can still pool at floor level beside the unit after a door is opened.

prompt: The same call requires brazing a liquid-line drier, then checking line voltage at a condensing-unit contactor. Which PPE approach matches both tasks?

options.text: Glasses for the braze only; skip gloves so recovery-hose nuts can be felt
A welding helmet for the braze, then no eye protection for the voltage check
Task PPE: shade and burn gear for brazing, then eye and hand protection for live voltage
A hard hat and ear plugs, which cover torch burns and electrical shock

explanation: NATE Core expects PPE matched to the hazard, not one outfit for the whole call. Brazing needs eye shade, gloves, and burn/fire protection. Voltage checks need eye protection and insulating gloves or tools rated for the circuit. Hearing protection and a hard hat do not stop torch burns, UV, or shock.

distractorExplanations.a: Skipping gloves during hose or fitting work invites frostbite or cuts; feeling nuts is not a reason to drop PPE.
distractorExplanations.b: A helmet for brazing does not excuse bare eyes at a live contactor; arc and debris still need eye protection.
distractorExplanations.d: Hard hats and hearing protection address impact and noise, not flame, UV, frostbite, or electrical contact.

prompt: A fused disconnect is mounted on the wall within sight of a rooftop condensing unit. What is that disconnect for during service?

options.text: To replace the branch-circuit breaker as the unit’s only overcurrent device
To drop 24 V control power while leaving line voltage on the contactor
To reset the compressor internal overload after a high-amp trip
To isolate the unit so it cannot be re-energized from a remote panel

explanation: A within-sight disconnect is a local isolation means so a tech can lock the equipment off and not have someone restore power from the indoor breaker. A non-fused switch provides no overcurrent protection. Opening only 24 V leaves lethal line voltage. Internal overloads reset thermally; they are not reset by the disconnect handle.

distractorExplanations.a: Many disconnects are non-fused; branch overcurrent stays at the breaker or fuses, not this handle.
distractorExplanations.b: The disconnect opens line voltage to the outdoor unit; killing only 24 V leaves the contactor live.
distractorExplanations.c: Compressor internal overloads reset after cooldown; the disconnect is isolation, not an overload reset.

prompt: A gas furnace rollout switch is open after a no-heat call. The heat exchanger is hot and soot is visible at the burner box. What should the technician do?

options.text: Stop, find the blockage or heat-exchanger/vent fault, and reset only after repair
Reset the rollout, watch two cycles, and replace the switch if it opens again
Raise manifold pressure so the flame is pulled back into the exchanger
Swap in a higher-temperature rollout so the nuisance trips stop

explanation: A rollout trip means flame left the heat exchanger—blocked flue, cracked exchanger, blower failure, or overfire. Diagnose and repair the cause; reset only when the path is safe. Repeated resets, higher gas pressure, or a hotter-rated switch hide a carbon monoxide and fire hazard.

distractorExplanations.b: A tripping rollout is usually doing its job; swapping it skips the vent or exchanger problem behind the trip.
distractorExplanations.c: Higher manifold pressure overfires the burner and can worsen rollout instead of pulling flame in.
distractorExplanations.d: A higher-rated switch defeats a flame-safety device and conceals the vent or exchanger fault.

prompt: Between jobs, refrigerant recovery cylinders and torch tanks ride in the service van. How should they be stored?

options.text: Valves open and uncapped so leftover vapor can bleed off in the cargo area
Capped, upright, secured, and kept within rating away from heat and flame
On their sides next to the lit torch kit so they are easy to grab
Refilled from each other in the van if a disposable DOT-39 can is empty

explanation: Cylinders remain pressure vessels even when they feel empty. Close valves, install caps, keep them upright and secured, and store them away from the torch, sun-baked van walls, and other heat. Open valves vent residual refrigerant and admit moisture. Heat and horizontal acetylene storage are overpressure and acetone hazards. Disposable cans are not refillable.

distractorExplanations.a: Open valves release residual refrigerant and let moisture in; empties are stored closed and capped.
distractorExplanations.c: Heat and flame next to cylinders can overpressurize them; they stay secured upright, away from the torch.
distractorExplanations.d: Disposable cylinders are not refillable in the field; that practice is both illegal and unsafe.

prompt: An installer must climb an extension ladder onto a low roof to reach a package unit, carrying a small tool pouch. What setup is required before the first step up?

options.text: Set a 1:1 angle so the ladder sits nearly vertical and saves rooftop space
Stop the rails flush with the eave so the ladder cannot slide past the roof
Set about a 4:1 angle, extend rails above the roof, and keep three-point contact
Stand on the top cap so both hands are free to pass tools onto the roof

explanation: Extension-ladder access to HVAC equipment follows a roughly 4:1 pitch (one foot out for every four feet of rise), rails extending above the landing, a secured base, and three-point contact. A vertical 1:1 set is tip-prone. Rails flush with the eave leave no handhold for the step-off. The top cap is not a standing surface.

distractorExplanations.a: A near-vertical set is unstable and easy to tip backward; the working pitch is about 4:1, not 1:1.
distractorExplanations.b: Rails need to extend above the roof so the tech has a handhold while stepping off; flush eaves are a fall setup.
distractorExplanations.d: The top cap and top step are not standing surfaces; three-point contact is lost if both feet are on the cap.

prompt: A 3-ton split just had a compressor burnout. The new compressor and liquid-line drier are in, and the tech is evacuating before charging. What deep-vacuum practice is the usual target?

options.text: Stop at 30 psig on the low-side manifold, then immediately add charge
Open shop air to 14.7 psia and treat that as a completed vacuum
Run the vacuum pump for two minutes with no gauge attached
Pull to 500 microns or lower and confirm the decay test holds

explanation: After a burnout, moisture and noncondensables must be pulled out, not guessed. Industry practice is a deep vacuum to about 500 microns (or lower) plus a decay test that holds, proving the system is tight and dry before refrigerant goes in.

distractorExplanations.a: 30 psig is a positive pressure, not a vacuum. Charging from there leaves air and moisture in the circuit.
distractorExplanations.b: 14.7 psia is atmospheric pressure. Shop air at that level is the opposite of an evacuation.
distractorExplanations.c: A two-minute pump-down with no micron gauge cannot show dryness or tightness; the reading and hold test are the proof.

prompt: A TXV cooling system is running. Suction pressure converts to 40°F saturation, and a clamp 6 inches from the compressor on the suction line reads 52°F. What superheat should be recorded?

options.text: 12°F: suction-line temperature minus saturated suction temperature
12°F: saturated suction temperature minus the suction-line reading
12°F of subcooling taken from those same suction-side numbers
12°F air-side split using 52°F supply minus 40°F return air

explanation: Superheat is how far actual suction-line temperature sits above saturation at the same pressure. 52°F minus 40°F is 12°F of superheat. The subtraction order matters; reversing it, using liquid-line subcooling, or mixing in air temperatures all report the wrong quantity.

distractorExplanations.b: Reversing the subtraction yields a negative number. Superheat is line temperature above saturation, not saturation minus the line.
distractorExplanations.c: Subcooling is taken on the liquid line against condensing saturation, not from suction pressure and a suction-line clamp.
distractorExplanations.d: Return-to-supply split is an air-side delta T. Those 40°F and 52°F figures are refrigerant saturation and suction-line temperature.

prompt: A tech is charging a condenser by subcooling. High-side pressure converts to 110°F saturation, and the liquid line leaving the outdoor coil reads 98°F. How is subcooling found?

options.text: 12°F of suction superheat using those liquid-line readings
12°F: saturated condensing temperature minus liquid-line temperature
Minus 12°F: liquid-line temperature minus saturated condensing temperature
12°F of discharge superheat leaving the compressor scroll

explanation: Subcooling is how far the liquid is cooled below condensing saturation at the measured high-side pressure. 110°F minus 98°F is 12°F of subcooling. That value is used to finish a weigh-adjustment or TXV charge by the manufacturer’s liquid-line target, not by suction or discharge superheat.

distractorExplanations.a: Superheat uses suction pressure and suction-line temperature. These numbers are high-side saturation and liquid-line temperature.
distractorExplanations.c: A properly subcooled liquid line is colder than saturation, so this order produces a negative value and the wrong sign.
distractorExplanations.d: Discharge superheat is compressor outlet temperature minus condensing saturation; it is not liquid subcooling leaving the coil.

prompt: On a running 2-ton heat pump in cooling, the tech hoses up a digital manifold and clips its thermistor on the suction line. What is that setup mainly for?

options.text: Reading deep vacuum in microns to prove the circuit is dry
Measuring total external static across the indoor blower
Converting pressures to saturation to compute superheat
Weighing how many pounds of refrigerant were added last visit

explanation: A digital manifold with a temperature clamp converts measured pressures to saturation on the PT chart and subtracts the clamped line temperature to give live superheat (or subcooling on the liquid line). That is a charging and diagnosis tool, not a micron, static, or scale instrument.

distractorExplanations.a: Compound gauges cannot resolve microns. Dehydration is confirmed with a dedicated micron gauge on the vacuum port.
distractorExplanations.b: TESP is an air-side manometer job with static probes in the ducts, not refrigerant hoses on the service valves.
distractorExplanations.d: Charge mass is read on a refrigerant scale. The manifold reports pressure and computed saturation, not pounds added.

prompt: An 80 kBtu/h natural-gas furnace is being commissioned. The tech taps a hose from the gas-valve manifold port to a manometer. What should that instrument be reading?

options.text: Manifold gas pressure of about 3.5 psig for natural gas
Deep-vacuum microns while the burners are firing
Flue-gas carbon monoxide in ppm at the draft hood
Manifold or inlet gas pressure in inches of water column

explanation: Residential natural-gas manifold pressure is a low water-column measurement (often about 3.5 in. WC), so a manometer—not a refrigerant psig gauge—is the right tool. Inlet pressure is also checked in inches WC against the valve rating before clocking the meter or setting offset.

distractorExplanations.a: 3.5 psig is far too high for a typical residential manifold; the common target is about 3.5 inches of water column.
distractorExplanations.b: Microns belong to evacuation of a refrigerant circuit. A firing furnace manometer is measuring gas pressure, not vacuum.
distractorExplanations.c: CO in ppm is a combustion-analyzer reading. A manometer measures pressure, not flue-gas concentration.

prompt: A packaged heat pump is loud at the indoor grill and the supply feels weak. The tech wants total external static pressure. How is TESP taken?

options.text: Supply plus return static at the air handler, blower running, filter in
Supply-plenum static only, blower on high, return probe left out
Static with the blower off so the manometer needles can settle
Static with the filter pulled to get a clean, unrestricted baseline

explanation: TESP is the sum of the supply and return static magnitudes at the air handler with the blower running and the system as it operates (filter installed). Compare that total to the blower’s rated external static. High TESP explains low airflow, noise, and coil freeze-up risk.

distractorExplanations.b: Supply static alone omits return restriction (filter, grille, duct). TESP needs both sides of the blower.
distractorExplanations.c: With the blower off there is no airflow, so static is essentially zero and says nothing about the duct system.
distractorExplanations.d: Pulling the filter lowers the reading and hides the restriction the customer actually runs with.

prompt: A 3-ton residential cooling coil is being set up. What rule-of-thumb airflow should the tech start from, then verify with instruments?

options.text: 250 CFM per ton as a universal humid-climate dehumidification rate
About 400 CFM per ton, then check split, static, or a flow method
550 CFM per ton because the indoor coil is also used for heating
800 CFM per ton so the evaporator surface cannot ice in cooling

explanation: Four hundred CFM per ton is the usual residential starting point (about 1,200 CFM on a 3-ton). Confirm it with temperature split, TESP versus the blower table, a flow hood, or a pressure-matching method. Do not leave airflow as a guess after charging.

distractorExplanations.a: Humid-climate setups may drop toward about 350 CFM/ton, not 250. That low a rate risks a frozen coil and poor capacity.
distractorExplanations.c: Heat-pump indoor airflow is still near 400 CFM/ton; 550 overshoots it and can cut heating supply temperature.
distractorExplanations.d: Doubling design airflow wrecks latent removal and raises static and noise. Ice is prevented near 400 CFM/ton, not 800.

prompt: A 230 V single-phase compressor is running in cooling. The tech puts a clamp-on ammeter around one run conductor. What comparison is that reading for?

options.text: Insulation resistance to ground in megohms while the motor runs
Running amps versus the locked-rotor amp rating to prove it is healthy
Running amps versus nameplate RLA or FLA under the present load
Winding ohms between C, S, and R with the clamp jaws closed

explanation: A clamp meter measures current while the compressor is loaded. Compare that amperage to rated load amps (or FLA on some motors), allowing for the actual voltage and operating pressures. High amps can mean overcharge, dirty condenser, or a failing motor; low amps can mean undercharge or a weak compressor.

distractorExplanations.a: Insulation to ground is a megohmmeter test with power locked out, not a live clamp-amp reading.
distractorExplanations.b: LRA is inrush with a locked rotor, several times running current. Steady running amps are judged against RLA, not LRA.
distractorExplanations.d: C-S-R winding resistance is an ohmmeter test on a de-energized motor. A clamp measures current, not ohms.

prompt: A cooling coil is moving air but the space stays humid. The tech brings a Bluetooth psychrometric probe to the return and supply. What is that tool for?

options.text: Refrigerant dew point so liquid-line subcooling can be calculated
Duct static pressure that proves a restricted return or dirty filter
Flue-gas temperature and oxygen used to set combustion efficiency
Wet-bulb and dry-bulb (or enthalpy) to judge airflow and capacity

explanation: A psychrometer measures air wet-bulb, dry-bulb, and the derived humidity and enthalpy. Comparing return to supply enthalpy shows whether the coil is doing sensible and latent work. That air-side picture is how you catch low latent capacity even when the blower is moving air.

distractorExplanations.a: Subcooling uses refrigerant high-side pressure and liquid-line temperature, not air-stream dew point from a psychrometer.
distractorExplanations.b: Static pressure is a manometer measurement. A psychrometric probe reads temperature and moisture, not inches of water.
distractorExplanations.c: Stack temperature and O2 are combustion-analyzer readings on a furnace or boiler, not a cooling-coil air test.

prompt: A tech is recovering R-410A from a 3-ton split into a 30 lb recovery cylinder on a scale. How must the cylinder be filled?

options.text: By weight, stopping before the cylinder’s rated fill limit (about 80%)
By weight, filling to 100 percent of the stamped water capacity
By pressure, stopping at 80 percent of the tank’s stamped rating
By sight, stopping when liquid shows at the vapor-valve port

explanation: Recovery cylinders are filled by weight so liquid has room to expand with temperature. Stay at or under the cylinder’s rated fill (commonly 80% of water capacity using the W.C. × 0.8 formula). Overfill is a rupture-disk or tank-failure hazard.

distractorExplanations.b: Filling to 100% of water capacity leaves no vapor space. Heat then raises hydrostatic pressure and can burst the cylinder.
distractorExplanations.c: Tank pressure tracks temperature, not liquid level. An 80% pressure reading is not a fill limit.
distractorExplanations.d: Liquid at the vapor valve means the tank is already liquid-full, past the safe fill, with no expansion space left.

prompt: After a burnout, power is locked out and the compressor leads are lifted. The tech connects an analog megohmmeter from a winding terminal to the shell. What is being checked?

options.text: Running amps against nameplate RLA while the megger is connected
Winding insulation resistance to ground on the megohm scale
Low-ohm winding-to-winding resistance among C, S, and R
Run-capacitor microfarads before the compressor is restarted

explanation: A megohmmeter applies a high test voltage and reads insulation resistance to ground in megohms. After a burnout that tells you whether windings are still isolated from the shell before a new start or a replace decision. It is not an amp, C-S-R ohm, or capacitor test.

distractorExplanations.a: RLA comparison is a clamp-on ammeter check on a running motor. A megger is used only with the circuit de-energized.
distractorExplanations.c: C-S-R winding resistance is a low-range ohmmeter measurement. The megger is for insulation to ground, not winding ohms.
distractorExplanations.d: Microfarads are read with a capacitance meter on a discharged capacitor, not with megohm insulation leads.

prompt: A 3-ton cooling system with a clean filter shows 75°F return and 70°F supply at the plenum. What does that far-too-low split usually mean?

options.text: A cracked heat exchanger mixing furnace gases into the supply air
A clogged condensate pan that is flooding and extra-cooling the coil
Too much airflow, or a coil that is undercharged or underperforming
Normal high-efficiency behavior, because a tiny split saves energy

explanation: A typical cooling split is about 16–22°F. Five degrees means the coil is removing little heat from the air: excess CFM, low charge, a weak compressor, or a restricted metering device. Measure airflow and refrigerant circuit before adding gas. Low airflow would raise the split, not collapse it.

distractorExplanations.a: A cracked heat exchanger is a heating-season combustion hazard. It does not explain a 5°F cooling delta T.
distractorExplanations.b: A clogged drain causes overflow or a float-switch shutdown, not a collapsed supply-to-return temperature split.
distractorExplanations.d: A very small split is lost capacity, not higher efficiency. The equipment is moving air without doing the cooling work.

prompt: An evaporator was replaced and the circuit is empty. The nameplate charge is 6.2 lb plus a line-set adder. How should the factory charge be put in?

options.text: Feed vapor until the suction line frosts all the way to the compressor
Add vapor until the liquid-line sight glass looks empty of bubbles
Copy last season’s invoice pounds onto the tank without a scale
Evacuate, then weigh the nameplate charge adjusted for line-set length

explanation: After a major repair the accurate residential method is a proper vacuum, then a weigh-in of the factory charge plus the manufacturer’s extra ounces per foot of liquid line. Superheat or subcooling is a check afterward, not a substitute for the scale on an empty system.

distractorExplanations.a: Frost to the compressor is an overcharge/flooding sign, not a weigh-in endpoint, and it risks slugging the compressor.
distractorExplanations.b: A clear or empty glass is a poor charge target on many TXV systems and does not replace weighing the nameplate amount.
distractorExplanations.c: Last year’s invoice may not match this line set or this repair. Charge mass has to be weighed for this system.

prompt: Supply air is weak and the blower sounds strained. The tech puts dual-port manometer probes immediately before and after the indoor coil. What does that reading show?

options.text: Air-side pressure drop that flags a dirty coil or restricted media
Airflow in CFM directly, with no fan table or flow hood needed
Refrigerant-side pressure drop from distributor to suction header
Total external static for the entire supply-and-return duct system

explanation: A dual-port manometer across one component reads that component’s air-side pressure drop. A high drop across the coil or filter means dirty media, a wet-clogged coil, or a blocked drain pan. Compare the drop to the manufacturer’s dirty-filter or coil limit.

distractorExplanations.b: A manometer reads inches of water, not CFM. Converting to airflow needs a fan table, coil table, or a true flow measurement.
distractorExplanations.c: Water-column probes are in the airstream. Refrigerant drop is read with gauge hoses on the refrigerant circuit.
distractorExplanations.d: TESP is supply plus return static at the air handler. One coil or filter drop is only that part’s share of the total.

prompt: A new gas cock is going onto black-iron pipe at a furnace. What thread sealant belongs on that joint?

options.text: Standard white PTFE plumbing tape, including on any flare nuts
A listed gas-rated compound or yellow tape on the male NPT threads
POE refrigerant oil brushed on the threads as a lubricant-sealant
Any general pipe dope packed onto the female threads for coverage

explanation: Gas NPT joints need a listed gas-rated pipe dope or gas-rated (typically yellow) PTFE tape on the male threads, sparing the first thread so compound is not pushed into the valve. Flare and union metal-to-metal faces get no tape. The listing is what makes the joint legal and leak-tight on fuel gas.

distractorExplanations.a: White plumbing tape is not the gas listing, and flare fittings seal metal to metal—tape on a flare is a leak path.
distractorExplanations.c: POE oil is for refrigerant flares and O-rings. It is not a listed fuel-gas thread sealant.
distractorExplanations.d: Dope on female threads is dragged into the gasway, and unlisted general dope may not be approved for fuel gas.

prompt: A PSC compressor nameplate calls for a 35 µF run capacitor; the failed part is marked 35 µF / 440 VAC. Which replacement is correct?

options.text: A 35 µF, 370 VAC part even though the original was marked 440 VAC
A 45 µF, 440 VAC part so the compressor gets extra starting torque
A 35 µF part rated 440 VAC or higher, matching the motor nameplate
Any nearby µF value if the replacement is stamped at least 370 VAC

explanation: Match the motor’s specified microfarads (typically within about ±10% or the OEM spec) and use a voltage rating equal to or higher than the original. A 440 V part can replace 370 V, but 370 V cannot replace 440 V. Raising µF increases winding current and heat instead of adding useful start torque.

distractorExplanations.a: Dropping the voltage rating from 440 V to 370 V overstresses the dielectric even if microfarads match.
distractorExplanations.b: Extra microfarads belong to start capacitors; an oversized run capacitor overheats the start winding.
distractorExplanations.d: Nearby µF values are not interchangeable; they change winding current and can damage the motor.

prompt: A 40 VA furnace transformer is too hot to hold after a few minutes of a cooling call. What does that usually mean?

options.text: 24 V on the secondary is supposed to run that hot under any load
An open high-pressure switch on Y has left the secondary unloaded
The 40 VA transformer is oversized for a 20 VA thermostat and relays
A shorted 24 V circuit, stuck relay, or overloaded VA rating

explanation: A control transformer overheats when secondary current is too high: a shorted 24 V wire, a stuck relay coil, or more VA than the transformer can supply. A correctly loaded 40 VA unit runs warm, not scalding. Opening a switch removes load and cools the transformer rather than heating it.

distractorExplanations.a: 24 V is the normal secondary; a healthy transformer at rated load is warm, not overheated.
distractorExplanations.b: An open safety on Y drops load off the secondary, so the transformer runs cooler, not hotter.
distractorExplanations.c: Serving 20 VA from 40 VA is half load; extra unused VA capacity does not cause overheating.

prompt: On a typical induced-draft gas furnace, when does the inducer motor run relative to ignition?

options.text: It pre-purges to prove draft, then runs through the burn as designed
It starts after flame is proven, pulling flue gas only once burners are lit
It runs only for the post-purge after the gas valve has already closed
It replaces the circulating blower and moves room air across the heat exchanger

explanation: The inducer pre-purges and must close the pressure switch before the control allows trial-for-ignition. It then stays on through the burn and usually post-purges. It moves combustion products through the heat exchanger; the indoor blower, not the inducer, moves conditioned air.

distractorExplanations.b: Ignition is locked out until draft is proven; the inducer is already running before the spark or hot surface igniter.
distractorExplanations.c: Post-purge is only one slice of the cycle; the inducer also pre-purges and runs during the entire burn.
distractorExplanations.d: The circulating blower moves supply air; the inducer is a combustion-vent motor, not a room-air mover.

prompt: A condensing-unit contactor has badly pitted, burned points and the compressor voltage sags when it pulls in. What is the correct repair?

options.text: File the points smooth and put the same contactor back in as routine service
Replace the contactor; pitted contacts add resistance and drop voltage
Leave it in place unless an ohmmeter shows the coil winding is open
Keep the pitted points and add a hard-start kit to overcome the sag

explanation: Pitted contacts raise resistance, drop voltage at the compressor terminals, and keep arcing. Replacement is the repair. Filing strips the silver facing and is only a short-term field patch. Coil continuity does not prove the power contacts are good, and a hard-start kit hides the voltage drop while the points keep burning.

distractorExplanations.a: Filing removes the contact plating and is a temporary patch; badly pitted contactors are replaced.
distractorExplanations.c: Coil continuity does not measure contact resistance; pitted power points can still drop voltage with a good coil.
distractorExplanations.d: A hard-start kit adds torque but leaves the high-resistance contacts in the circuit to keep degrading.

prompt: A compressor uses a start capacitor with a potential relay. When should that start capacitor stay in the circuit?

options.text: Continuously, in series with the start winding the same way a run capacitor is used
Through start and run, left paralleled with the run capacitor for the whole cycle
Only during start, then dropped out by the relay or PTC once the motor is up
Only after the motor is at speed, so it can correct running power factor

explanation: Start capacitors are intermittent-duty. A potential relay or PTC takes them out of the circuit once the motor approaches speed. Left in during run they overheat and fail. Continuous phase shift and power-factor correction are the run capacitor’s job, not the start capacitor’s.

distractorExplanations.a: That wiring describes a run capacitor; start capacitors are not continuous-duty and fail if left in circuit.
distractorExplanations.b: A hard-start kit parallels the run capacitor only for start; it must drop out or the start capacitor cooks.
distractorExplanations.d: Running power-factor correction is the run capacitor’s role; the start capacitor adds torque during start only.

prompt: You are wiring a new heat-pump thermostat and need to know when the reversing-valve solenoid is energized. What is the right check?

options.text: Assume heating on every brand because the valve fails safe into cooling
Feed the solenoid 240 V from the contactor so it tracks compressor run
Energize it in both modes; defrost simply turns the solenoid off to reverse flow
Energize it in one mode and confirm O versus B on the OEM diagram

explanation: Most split heat pumps energize the reversing valve in cooling (thermostat O). Some brands energize in heating (B). The solenoid is a 24 V coil, not a line-voltage load on the contactor. Read the outdoor-unit diagram rather than guessing fail-safe polarity.

distractorExplanations.a: Some OEMs use B (energize in heat), but many use O (energize in cool); fail-safe polarity is not universal.
distractorExplanations.b: The reversing-valve coil is 24 V from O/B, not 240 V paralleled with the compressor contactor.
distractorExplanations.c: The valve is powered in only one mode; defrost drives it to the cooling position, which may be on or off by brand.

prompt: A furnace board flashes a pressure-switch fault on a call for heat and never tries ignition. What should you check first?

options.text: Inducer operation, vent and intake, and the hose to the pressure switch
The flame rod, treating the flash as a failed flame-prove after ignition
The high-limit switch and blower wheel, as if the code were a limit trip
Gas-valve outlet pressure on a manometer before looking at the vent

explanation: A pressure-switch fault means the control did not see the inducer prove draft. Check inducer spin, blocked or disconnected vent/intake, a cracked or water-logged hose, and the switch itself. Flame sense, limits, and gas pressure are later in the sequence and are not energized until the switch closes.

distractorExplanations.b: The flame sensor proves flame after ignition; this code is about draft proof before the trial for ignition.
distractorExplanations.c: A high-limit trip is a different code; a pressure-switch fault points at the inducer and vent path.
distractorExplanations.d: The gas valve is not powered until the pressure switch closes, so manometer work skips the draft circuit.

prompt: A clamp meter on a compressor run lead shows locked-rotor amps that never fall after the contactor closes. What does that mean?

options.text: Normal inrush that is allowed to sit at LRA for a couple of minutes
The compressor or outdoor fan is not starting; the rotor is locked
A high-efficiency scroll drawing full-load current that looks like LRA
A normal current spike while the heat pump is in an active defrost

explanation: Locked-rotor amps last only for a fraction of a second on a successful start, then current falls toward RLA. LRA that holds means the rotor is not turning: open start circuit, failed capacitor, or a seized compressor or fan. Kill power and diagnose before the windings overheat.

distractorExplanations.a: Healthy inrush collapses in well under a second; sustained LRA is a locked rotor, not a timed warm-up.
distractorExplanations.c: A motor at full load draws about RLA, which is far below locked-rotor amps on the nameplate.
distractorExplanations.d: Defrost does not pin the compressor at LRA; running current in defrost still sits near RLA.

prompt: At a conventional 24 V thermostat sub-base, what do terminals R and C supply?

options.text: 24 V hot and the cooling call that drives the outdoor contactor coil
120 V hot and neutral taken straight off the furnace transformer primary
24 V hot and common from the control-transformer secondary
24 V hot and the reversing-valve output used on heat-pump O or B

explanation: R is the hot side of the 24 V transformer secondary and C is the common return. Powered thermostats and many controls need both. Y is the cooling call, O/B is reversing-valve, and 120 V belongs on the transformer primary—not on the thermostat terminals.

distractorExplanations.a: The cooling call to the contactor is Y; C is the common return of the 24 V secondary, not the Y output.
distractorExplanations.b: 120 V feeds the transformer primary; R and C are the 24 V secondary leads, not line voltage.
distractorExplanations.d: Reversing-valve output is O or B; C is the common side of the control circuit, not a valve feed.

prompt: A furnace transformer secondary is described as floating (ungrounded). How should you treat the C connection?

options.text: Bond C to the suction line so refrigerant piping becomes the ground point
Leave C disconnected at the board so the secondary stays fully floating
Ground both R and C secondary legs to keep the 24 V circuit balanced
Follow the OEM grounding and C landing so safeties and Wi-Fi stats work

explanation: “Floating” does not mean C is unused. Land common where the schematic shows, including any OEM chassis ground of one secondary leg. Powered thermostats and many flame/safety circuits need that defined common. Bonding to piping or grounding both legs creates faults.

distractorExplanations.a: Refrigerant piping is not a control-circuit grounding electrode; follow the furnace schematic, not the suction line.
distractorExplanations.b: C is still required for powered stats and many safeties; a floating secondary still uses its common lead.
distractorExplanations.c: Grounding both secondary legs shorts the transformer through earth and typically blows the 24 V fuse.

prompt: An outdoor condensing unit hums when the contactor pulls in, but the compressor never starts. What should you check first?

options.text: Indoor filter loading only, treating the hum as a return-air restriction
The run or start capacitor and a possible seized compressor
Whether the liquid-line drier was installed with the flow arrow reversed
Suction-line insulation thickness before any electrical or amp test

explanation: Hum-no-start is a classic open or weak capacitor or a locked compressor. Confirm voltage at the terminals, check capacitor µF, and feel whether the compressor is trying to turn. Airflow, driers, and insulation do not make a compressor hum in place of starting.

distractorExplanations.a: A dirty indoor filter can trip high pressure after a start, but it does not keep a humming compressor from starting.
distractorExplanations.c: A reversed drier is a restriction after the unit is running; it does not produce a hum-no-start at the compressor.
distractorExplanations.d: Suction insulation affects heat gain on the line; it is not a start-circuit or seized-rotor diagnosis.

prompt: A heat-pump outdoor board is in defrost. What typically ends that defrost cycle?

options.text: The indoor coil sensor reaching a comfort termination temperature
Outdoor coil termination temperature or a time-limit backup
Outdoor air rising above the auxiliary-heat balance-point setting
The board’s 30/60/90-minute pin timing out while still in defrost

explanation: Defrost ends when the outdoor coil (or liquid-line) sensor rises to the termination temperature, or when a time-limit backup expires if the coil stays cold. The indoor coil is not the defrosted surface. Balance point controls auxiliary heat, and the 30/60/90 pins set time between defrost checks, not the end of an active defrost.

distractorExplanations.a: Defrost clears ice from the outdoor coil; an indoor-coil temperature is not the termination input.
distractorExplanations.c: Balance point governs auxiliary-heat lockout and staging, not when an active defrost ends.
distractorExplanations.d: Those pins set the interval between defrost attempts, not the maximum length of the defrost that is already running.

prompt: A communicating or PWM furnace ECM blower will not run on a call for heat even though line voltage is present at the motor. What is usually missing?

options.text: A run capacitor and speed taps on the motor’s line-voltage leads, as on a PSC
A separate variable-frequency drive mounted in the furnace control panel
An OEM PWM, serial, or 24 V tap command plus line voltage
Line voltage alone, with speed set only by an internal motor thermistor

explanation: ECM modules need a command from the furnace control—PWM, serial, or discrete 24 V taps—plus correct line voltage and a good common. They do not use a PSC run capacitor. Drive electronics sit in the motor module, not a panel VFD, and line power by itself does not set torque or speed.

distractorExplanations.a: That describes a PSC blower; ECMs have no run capacitor and are commanded by a low-voltage or serial signal.
distractorExplanations.b: ECM inverter electronics are inside the motor end module; residential furnaces do not add a separate panel VFD.
distractorExplanations.d: Line voltage powers the module; without the control’s command signal the motor typically will not run.

prompt: A new Wi-Fi thermostat keeps dropping offline on a furnace with no unused C conductor at the wall. What is the clean fix?

options.text: Jumper R to C at the thermostat so it can draw continuous 24 V power
Feed R and C from a plug-in 120 V adapter to power the Wi-Fi radio
Replace the batteries and treat C as optional backup for the display
Add a C wire or an approved power extender per the OEM docs

explanation: Wi-Fi stats need a real 24 V common. Run a C wire, use a spare conductor, or install an OEM-approved power extender / common maker. Jumping R to C shorts the transformer. 120 V on R/C destroys the control. Batteries do not stop power-stealing dropouts.

distractorExplanations.a: Jumping R to C shorts the 24 V secondary and typically blows the control fuse or the transformer.
distractorExplanations.b: R and C are 24 V control terminals; applying 120 V destroys the thermostat and often the furnace board.
distractorExplanations.c: C supplies continuous 24 V for the radio; batteries do not keep a power-stealing Wi-Fi thermostat online.

prompt: You are installing a fused disconnect at a split-system condensing unit. How should the fuse size be chosen?

options.text: From the unit nameplate maximum fuse or HACR breaker rating
Equal to the minimum circuit ampacity printed on the nameplate
At 125 percent of compressor RLA, ignoring the outdoor fan motor
Equal to the compressor locked-rotor amps listed on the nameplate

explanation: Overcurrent protection at the condensing unit follows the nameplate maximum fuse or HACR circuit-breaker rating. Minimum circuit ampacity sizes the conductors, not the fuses. Using 125% of compressor RLA alone leaves out other loads, and fusing at LRA provides almost no protection.

distractorExplanations.b: MCA sizes the branch-circuit conductors; fuses are taken from the nameplate maximum overcurrent device.
distractorExplanations.c: 125% of RLA is part of the MCA wire-sizing math and is not the fuse or breaker rating by itself.
distractorExplanations.d: LRA is far above the allowed overcurrent rating; fusing at LRA leaves the conductors essentially unprotected.

prompt: A homeowner points at a 410A condenser and says, "Just add a pound — the last tech always did." You have not connected gauges. What should you do?

options.text: Diagnose with gauges, temperatures, and airflow before changing the charge
Add the pound because a small 410A top-off is acceptable on residential splits
Watch suction pressure only and add refrigerant if the gauge reads under 100 psig
Recover the entire charge first and weigh in the nameplate amount before any tests

explanation: Charge is a measured decision, not a courtesy pound. Superheat or subcooling plus confirmed airflow show whether refrigerant is actually the fault. Adding gas blind can overcharge a 410A system and hide airflow, restriction, or metering problems.

distractorExplanations.b: A "harmless" top-off is a common myth; unmeasured 410A can overcharge the coil and raise head pressure.
distractorExplanations.c: Suction pressure alone does not show charge; you still need temperatures and correct airflow for SH/SC.
distractorExplanations.d: Jumping to full recovery skips diagnosis; testing first shows whether charge is the problem at all.

prompt: The next technician on a compressor callback finds no model, serial, pressures, or part numbers on yesterday's ticket. Why does that documentation matter?

options.text: EPA requires those fields on every residential service invoice, no exceptions
NATE audits each technician's tickets before it will renew the credential
The following tech and the warranty both need a traceable service record
A warranty claim is complete if the invoice shows only the dollar total

explanation: A complete ticket protects the customer, the shop, and the next person on the job. Model, serial, readings, and what was replaced let a warranty claim and a callback diagnosis start from facts instead of guesswork.

distractorExplanations.a: EPA recordkeeping targets refrigerant disposal and larger appliances, not a full ticket on every house call.
distractorExplanations.b: NATE recertification uses CE hours or retesting, not an audit of a technician's service tickets.
distractorExplanations.d: An invoice total proves payment, not the failed part, serial, or operating conditions a claim needs.

prompt: The outdoor fan motor is open. The replacement will not arrive until tomorrow, and the house is occupied. How should you leave the job today?

options.text: Jumper the high-pressure switch so the compressor can run without the fan overnight
Leave the system running as found so they keep some cooling until the part arrives
Recover the charge and leave the manifold hoses on the ports until you return
Make the equipment safe, explain options and price, and schedule the follow-up

explanation: If you cannot finish, leave the equipment in a safe state and tell the owner what happens next. Defeating a safety or running a failed condenser overnight trades a callback for a compressor failure and liability.

distractorExplanations.a: Bypassing a high-pressure switch so the compressor runs without a fan is a fire and equipment hazard.
distractorExplanations.b: Leaving a known-failed condenser running can overheat the compressor and still leave the house without reliable cooling.
distractorExplanations.c: Gauges left on ports invite leaks and tampering, and the customer still has no price or return time.

prompt: At the supply house a helper is refused a 25 lb cylinder of R-410A because they have no card. What does an EPA 608 certification actually allow?

options.text: Buy and handle regulated refrigerants and recover them from appliances
Install line-voltage wiring from a disconnect to a new condensing unit
Pull gas permits and install furnaces under the local mechanical code
Purchase factory-sealed window air conditioners for rental properties

explanation: Section 608 is a federal refrigerant-handling credential. It is what supply houses check before selling regulated refrigerant and what authorizes recovery from appliances. It is not an electrician, gas, or contractor license.

distractorExplanations.b: Line-voltage work is governed by electrical licensing and code, not by an EPA 608 card.
distractorExplanations.c: Furnace permits and gas installs fall under local mechanical licensing, not EPA 608.
distractorExplanations.d: Factory-sealed room units can be sold without 608; the card governs refrigerant purchase and recovery.

prompt: A 14-year-old heat pump still cools, but the matching furnace has a confirmed cracked heat exchanger and CO in the living space. When is recommending a new system appropriate?

options.text: Any time the outdoor unit is over 10 years old, even if the repair is a cheap capacitor
When the equipment is unsafe or uneconomic, and you show the owner the facts
When a repair quote exceeds 25 percent of replacement, even before diagnosis
Any time the unit uses R-22, because repairing R-22 systems is now illegal

explanation: Replacement advice follows documented safety and economics, not age quotas. A cracked exchanger with CO in occupied space is an unsafe keep-it-running situation; you present findings and options, including replacement, instead of selling on age alone.

distractorExplanations.a: Age by itself does not justify replacement; a cheap repair on a still-safe unit should be offered first.
distractorExplanations.c: A percentage rule before diagnosis is a sales shortcut, not a finding-based recommendation.
distractorExplanations.d: R-22 production ended, but servicing existing R-22 systems with reclaimed or stocked refrigerant remains legal.

prompt: A homeowner shows phone photos of rust streaks they believe are a cracked heat exchanger. The furnace is still running. What should you do first?

options.text: Disregard the photos, because a combustion analyzer is required to confirm a crack
Red-tag the furnace from the photos without opening the cabinet yourself
Inspect, confirm, shut the furnace down if unsafe, and document in writing
Quote a heat-exchanger replacement immediately because photos are proof

explanation: Customer photos are a lead, not a condemnation. You inspect, confirm with visual or camera work and combustion checks, shut the furnace down if it is unsafe, and put the finding in writing so the owner has a clear next step.

distractorExplanations.a: Photos are worth checking; visual inspection and combustion testing together confirm a crack, not analyzer-only dismissal.
distractorExplanations.b: Condemning equipment needs your own confirmation; a rust photo can be a stain, not a crack.
distractorExplanations.d: Ordering a heat exchanger from a phone picture skips confirmation and can sell a part that is not needed.

prompt: You recorded 8°F subcooling on a 410A TXV system this morning. The afternoon tech recorded 22°F and added two pounds. The numbers still conflict. What is the professional move?

options.text: Follow the senior technician's reading and add charge to match that measurement
Split the difference and add half of the refrigerant the other tech recommended
Trust the newer digital manifold and ignore the analog gauges from the morning
Re-measure superheat, subcooling, airflow, and the nameplate before adding more

explanation: Charge disputes are settled with shared measurements, not seniority or new tools. Re-check SH/SC with confirmed airflow against the nameplate target before adding more 410A, or you stack two wrong charges on top of each other.

distractorExplanations.a: Seniority is not a measurement; the disagreement is resolved by re-testing SH/SC and airflow together.
distractorExplanations.b: A compromise amount is not a diagnosis and can still leave the system over- or undercharged.
distractorExplanations.c: Tool age does not settle a charge dispute; both techs re-measure against the same nameplate target.

prompt: A homeowner asks you to leave the filter rack empty "so the air handler can breathe" year-round. What should you do?

options.text: Explain coil and blower damage and IAQ risk, and leave a proper filter in place
Remove the filter as requested because the customer owns the equipment and signed
Slide in a 1-inch MERV 16 so they get cleaner air with supposedly freer airflow
Pull the filter and promise yearly coil cleaning to replace continuous filtration

explanation: A filter protects the coil, blower, and indoor air. Permanent removal is not a performance upgrade. Explain the damage and IAQ risk and leave a correctly sized, reasonable-MERV filter in the rack.

distractorExplanations.b: Ownership does not make an unsafe request good practice; dirt will load the coil and blower.
distractorExplanations.c: A high-MERV 1-inch filter raises static and cuts airflow; it does not "free" the blower.
distractorExplanations.d: Annual coil cleaning does not stop debris loading the blower between visits; filtration is still required.

prompt: While rolling a furnace across a hallway, you gouge a hardwood floor. Nobody else saw it. What should you do?

options.text: Patch the floor yourself after hours before telling the shop or owner
Notify the shop and the customer now and follow the company's claim policy
Tell dispatch only and let the office contact the owner about a claim later
Hide a note on the invoice and wait for the customer to raise the damage

explanation: Property damage is disclosed the same visit. Tell the shop and the customer, then follow the company's claim path. Hidden repairs and delayed office calls look like concealment and usually cost more than an honest report.

distractorExplanations.a: A secret after-hours patch skips insurance and claim procedure and destroys trust if the repair fails.
distractorExplanations.c: The customer should hear about the gouge from you on site, not from the office days later.
distractorExplanations.d: Fine print on an invoice is not disclosure; damage is reported directly and immediately.

prompt: A coworker wants a social-media photo of the new thermostat showing the homeowner's PIN and street number. What is the correct handling of that information?

options.text: The post is fine if you crop the customer's last name out of the photo
The post is fine once the job is finished and the invoice has been paid
It is a privacy failure; do not post customer credentials or addresses
The post is fine if you blur the house number but leave the PIN visible

explanation: Thermostats, Wi-Fi logins, PINs, and addresses are customer credentials. They stay off social media even after the job is paid. Cropping a surname or blurring a house number still leaks access to the home's controls.

distractorExplanations.a: The PIN is still an access code; omitting a last name does not make posting it acceptable.
distractorExplanations.b: Payment status does not change privacy duties; credentials are not content for a job-site post.
distractorExplanations.d: Blurring the address leaves the PIN exposed, and the PIN itself grants control of the system.

prompt: A no-heat call is a tripped furnace breaker. The blower had been humming before the trip. What should the visit still include?

options.text: Install the next larger breaker so the furnace stops those nuisance trips
Reset it, confirm heat at a register, and tell them to call if it trips again
Swap the breaker because any trip is proof that the device has worn out
Find the overload or short that caused the trip before resetting and leaving

explanation: A breaker trip is a symptom. A humming blower plus a trip points to an overloaded motor, short, or wiring fault. Find that cause before a reset-and-leave, or the next trip can be a fire instead of a callback.

distractorExplanations.a: Breakers protect the wire; upsizing hides the fault and can overheat the circuit.
distractorExplanations.b: Resetting without a cause turns a diagnostic visit into a delayed failure.
distractorExplanations.c: Most trips are overload or short; swapping the breaker leaves the real fault in place.

prompt: You are writing a repair estimate for a locked compressor on a residential split. What should the quote include?

options.text: Recovery, filter-drier, evacuation, start components, the compressor, and labor
Compressor and labor only, with recovery and the drier billed on the final invoice
Part and labor only, because a replacement compressor ships with a new drier
Compressor, drier, and labor, reusing the old charge without a proper evacuation

explanation: A compressor change is a refrigerant circuit repair. The honest estimate includes recovery, a new drier, evacuation, start components, the compressor, and labor so the owner sees the real cost before you start, not as surprise add-ons.

distractorExplanations.b: Billing required recovery and a drier later hides the true cost and starts a billing fight.
distractorExplanations.c: Replacement compressors do not include a filter-drier; that is a separate required part.
distractorExplanations.d: Reusing the old charge skips recovery and evacuation and leaves acid and moisture in the circuit.

prompt: A furnace swap needs a larger gas pipe. Your license covers HVAC equipment, not fuel-gas piping in this city. What should you do?

options.text: Run the short black-iron resize yourself, claiming the HVAC license covers it
Stop the piping and have a licensed plumber or gas fitter complete the resize
Install a larger gas valve so the undersized supply pipe can stay as built
Complete the resize and skip the permit because the ticket is tagged service

explanation: Work stays inside the license the city actually issued. If fuel-gas piping is a plumber or fitter ticket, you stop that portion and bring in the right trade. Run length, "service" labels, and valve swaps do not create a piping license.

distractorExplanations.a: A short run does not change licensing; gas piping still needs the credential this city requires.
distractorExplanations.c: A larger gas valve cannot fix an undersized supply line; the pipe itself has to be resized.
distractorExplanations.d: Calling the visit a service call does not waive piping licenses or permit rules.

prompt: A clerk at permit intake treats your NATE Core wallet card as a contractor license. What should you tell the customer?

options.text: NATE Core is the state contractor license for HVAC installation and service
NATE Core is the federal refrigerant exam that replaces the EPA 608 card
NATE Core is an industry knowledge exam, not a license that authorizes permits
NATE Core is a brand warranty class required to install specific equipment

explanation: NATE Core tests installation and service fundamentals. It is a voluntary industry certification. Permits and legal HVAC work still require the state or local contractor license, and refrigerant handling still requires EPA 608.

distractorExplanations.a: Contractor licensing is issued by states or localities; NATE does not replace that license.
distractorExplanations.b: EPA 608 is a separate federal requirement; passing NATE Core does not substitute for it.
distractorExplanations.d: NATE is brand-neutral and independent; it is not a manufacturer warranty course.

prompt: Capacitor and contactor are replaced. How should you close the site before you leave?

options.text: Reinstall the panels but leave gauges on the ports to watch charge overnight
Bag the old parts but leave the blower door off so the indoor motor can cool
Show cool air at a register and leave packaging in the driveway for the owner
Reinstall panels, remove scraps, and confirm the system runs in the called mode

explanation: A finished call is assembled, cleaned up, and demonstrated. Panels go back on, scraps leave with you, and the customer sees the system run in the mode they called about so you catch an open door switch or a dead capacitor before you drive away.

distractorExplanations.a: Gauges left on ports are a leak path and a tampering risk; they come off before you leave.
distractorExplanations.b: An open blower door defeats the interlock and pulls unfiltered air across the coil.
distractorExplanations.c: Leaving packaging in the drive is unfinished cleanup and can be a trip or wind hazard.
